Last Wednesday, I had the privilege of speaking at NJIT's "Shaping the Future of Healthcare & Innovation" dinner alongside Dr. Genoa R. Warner, PhD and Dr. Bryan Pfister, PhD.

I shared my work designing peptide therapeutics in Dr. Vivek Kumar's lab, including the multiple sclerosis project that was published this summer. I also talked about being an EMT--on the ambulance, medicine is about the next ten minutes; in the lab, it is about the next ten years. Translational medicine sits between the two, and that is where I want to spend my career.

At dinner after the presentations, I sat with Ray Chan, Michelle Cirillo, Mark Bagarazzi, John Pelesko, and Jack Shea, and we talked the whole night. Being the only undergraduate student at the dinner surprisingly was not too uncomfortable! I was really enjoying the conversation and topics that we talked about, and to me, this dinner was one of many signs that I am on the right career path. I could see many dinners like this in the future... Getting a treatment from the lab to a patient takes scientists, doctors, and people who believe in the work early on, and nights like this are where they meet.

Thank you to Dean Louis Hamilton for recommending me and for the introduction, and to everyone who came over to talk afterward!

New Jersey Institute of Technology | Albert Dorman Honors College at NJIT

Earlier this month, the Journal of Young Investigators (JYI) executive board came together in Seattle for our annual in-person summit!

This was my second summit, and as the 22nd Editor-in-Chief, it is always rewarding to step back and look at the whole journal at once. We spent Saturday going through every department’s year in review, the challenges ahead, and the plans to tackle them. Near the end of the day, we went through who is graduating this spring, which is a big part of running a journal that is entirely student-led.

That turnover is something our team has thought about a lot. Back in April at the Council on Undergraduate Research's NCUR, we presented a poster on what we called “knowledge drain”: when experienced members graduate, much of what they know leaves with them. Our approach has been to build structure into the journal, with a multi-stage hiring process, asynchronous onboarding that works across time zones, tiered training, and a shared workflow board for every manuscript.

This year put that system to the test, and I’m proud of how the team grew:
- 👥 Staff Growth: 27 new members joined from 96 applications
- 🔬 Higher Standards: every manuscript now goes to two associate editors and a research editor, with a two-week review window, and we published an AI policy for both authors and reviewers
- 🌍 Increased Access: we reestablished our translations department, brought back Perspective articles, and are developing partnerships for undergraduate research events

In 2027, JYI turns 30! I look forward to seeing where we go in the next year

A massive thank you to the editorial board for everything they carry:
- Hallel Abrams Gerber, Managing Editor
- Julian Lau, Senior Research Editor
- Manjushree Balaji, Senior News and Careers Editor
- Jinglan Liang, Translations Coordinator

Thank you as well to Amrutha Alibilli, and the rest of the corporate board (including the famous Cindy Wu), and to Nafisa Jadavji, PhD, FAHA, and the Board of Directors for their continued guidance.

On a lighter note, the very last item on our agenda was cleaning the Airbnb exactly to the host’s instructions. Thankfully, a house full of editors knows how to follow a style guide! 🧹

Earlier this month, the American Association of Physicians of Indian Origin (AAPI)'s American Association of Physicians of Indian Origin MSRF and National AAPI PreMed - American Association of Physicians of Indian Origin's Premedical Sections hosted our 2026 Fall Virtual Research Symposium, and as the Research Chair, I once again had the pleasure of helping organize and host it!

This year, presenters joined us from the US and abroad, with 11 presentations covering the whole road from bench to bedside: translational work testing a hydrogel treatment for degenerated spinal discs, a study of workplace violence against healthcare workers in India, and a pediatric lung malformation masquerading as tubercular pneumonia.
Recruiting judges took a lot of outreach this year, so I’m especially grateful to the seven physicians who said yes and gave up part of their Saturday to score and give feedback!

Last year I MC’d the symposium on my own, and this year I had the pleasure of co-MCing alongside Maneeth Mylavarapu! A big shoutout as well to Dr. Sohi Mistry, whose support and leadership on the MSRF side made this possible.

Like last year, this was a true team effort. A massive thank you to our research team for reviewing abstracts and running the day, and to every presenter who shared their work with us!

Next up: the AAPI Medical Scholars Summit 2027 on Saturday, April 3rd in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. The call for speakers is now open, and I hope to see many of you there!

Albert Dorman Honors College at NJIT
